extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of physics and philosophy of science (readers of a foundations-of-mechanics textbook)
extracted.subtask_description: Explication and conceptual formulation of general laws governing corpuscles/particles (first through fourth laws, mass, inertia, and methodological cautions) as presented in a foundations-of-mechanics textbook. Focuses on how to construct conceptual models, assumptions to make, and limits of applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: First general law of motion (every corpuscle influences every other)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every corpuscle in the conceptual model of the universe must be conceived as moving with due regard to the presence of every other corpuscle, although for very distant corpuscles the regard paid is extremely small as compared with that paid to immediate neighbours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: individual corpuscles 'dance' in groups and influence one another at all distances; practical modelling allows the influence to be negligible at great separations. Example/extension: probably applies to prime-atoms through particles; alternative formulation: influence may act via adjacent ether-elements, so 'Every corpuscle, whether of ether or gross "matter" influences the motion of the adjacent ether corpuscles, and through them of every other corpuscle, however distant; the influence thus spread is nevertheless very insignificant at great as compared with small distances.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological rule: neglect influences beyond measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: In constructing conceptual models of the universe we neglect influences which even in the aggregate are beyond our powers of measurement, and purposely exclude slight variations of motion due to more distant groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: isolate a particular group of corpuscles (or the most limited field, a single corpuscle) for conceptual discussion. This justifies treating many-body problems by focusing on dominant local interactions and ignoring negligible distant effects when building usable mechanical descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second law / Principle of inertia
rubrics_metrics.description: The characteristic of corpuscles that they do not alter their uniform motion except in the presence of other corpuscles; if a corpuscle is isolated (or considered in the limit of negligible mutual influence) it will remain at rest relative to another or continue to move with the same speed in the same direction (uniform motion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: inertia is the property that a corpuscle will not 'dance' (alter motion) unless it has partners to dance with. Caveat: applicability to ether-elements is unclear; for gross 'matter' the law flows from structure of prime-atom (i.e., may be emergent rather than fundamental for ether). Example: isolated vortex-ring in an infinite fluid moves uniformly (see cited hydrodynamics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Third law: mutual accelerations determined by relative position
rubrics_metrics.description: The mutual accelerations (the 'spurt and shunt' of velocities) of two corpuscles are determined by their relative position; mutual accelerations have the same direction but opposite senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical assumption for particles of gross 'matter': accelerations act in the line joining the corpuscles and depend solely on relative position. Caveats: may fail for ether-elements or structured prime-atoms; in many phenomena (especially involving fluid/ether) mutual acceleration may also depend on velocities relative to each other or to the ether.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direction-of-action assumption (line joining particles)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is usually assumed that the action between particles at a distance is to be considered as taking place in the line joining them and as depending only on relative position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicability: often correct enough for particles of gross 'matter' and non-adjacent particles; may be invalid for phenomena where representing particles as points is inappropriate (e.g., certain chemical/physical effects), or for ether-elements where the notion of the joining line vanishes with continuity. The assumption may flow from the particular internal structure (vortex-ring vs ether-squirt) of prime-atoms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat: possible dependence on relative velocity
rubrics_metrics.description: Mutual accelerations of corpuscles may be influenced not only by relative position but also by their velocities (relative to each other or to the ether); introducing velocity dependence is not necessarily incompatible with conservation of energy so long as all components (e.g., fluid/ether) are accounted for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: two bodies moving in a fluid appear to accelerate each other depending on velocities; neglecting the fluid makes accelerations appear velocity-dependent while total system (fluid + bodies) still conserves energy. Implication: caution when modelling electromagnetism or magneto-electric phenomena by pure position-dependent action-at-a-distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle: accelerations of elements depend on positions (general statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether dealing with continuous ether or discontinuous atoms and molecules, if we fix attention on an element the acceleration (not the velocity) of this point will depend on the position of this point or element relative to other points or elements (and possibly in certain cases on its velocities relative to those points or elements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General formulation synthesizing prior caveats: for particles of gross 'matter' it is generally sufficient to assert dependence solely on position, but the possibility of velocity-dependence is acknowledged for other contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Velocity as epitome of past history (determinism and the meaning of force)
rubrics_metrics.description: The given velocities of a system at any time may be looked upon as the sum of the past changes of motion; the causes of a given motion can only be conceived as lying in the totality of all past relative positions of the system. Thus force, as the conceptual idea of moving cause, could only be defined as the history of the relative positions of a system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: if one knows actual velocities and how accelerations depend on relative position (and possibly velocities), then theoretically one can trace the whole past or future history of the conceptual model of the universe. Practical limitations: human computational incapacity, but astronomers successfully use this idea to compute past eclipses and infer historical chronology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourth law / Kinetic Scale (constancy of acceleration ratio)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ratio of the acceleration of A due to B to the acceleration of B due to A must always be considered to be the same whatever be the position of A and B, and whatever be the surrounding field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: by measuring mutual accelerations across many experiments one finds that Qt and Q't' (accelerations of A due to B and B due to A) maintain a fixed ratio characteristic of the pair. This yields the concept that the ratio depends on the individual pair of corpuscles and not on their position or surrounding field; experimental justification comes from observations on perceptual bodies across varied fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific definition of mass
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass of a corpuscle A (relative to a standard corpuscle Q) is defined as Mass_of_A = (Acceleration of Q due to A) / (Acceleration of A due to Q); mass is a relative numerical ratio of accelerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: mass is relative (depends on chosen standard) and is a number representing a ratio of accelerations rather than 'quantity of matter.' This is the scientific operational definition; textbooks defining mass as 'quantity of matter' are criticized as idle. Practical note: to avoid measuring every pair, choose a standard corpuscle Q and record ratios of accelerations of Q with each corpuscle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability caveat: limitations when extending particle-laws to ether
rubrics_metrics.description: Many of the laws postulated for particles (e.g., action along the joining line, inertia, position-only dependence) may not apply unchanged to ether-elements; ether-continuity/discontinuity and the internal structure of prime-atoms may alter the form of interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: if the ether is absolutely continuous the line joining adjacent elements vanishes, making some particle-based descriptions meaningless; discontinuous ether might permit analogous laws but reintroduce problems that the ether-concept was meant to solve. Conclusion: be cautious in extending particle-based mechanical laws across all corpuscle scales.
